quests.d: Scope the prompt, do the napkin math, design the two API calls, and choose 301 or 302
quests.goal: Your win today: in the first five minutes you can ask the right scoping questions, work out about 1,160 writes/s, 11,600 reads/s, 365 billion records and 36.5 TB, name the two endpoints, and say when you'd use 301 vs 302.
quests.bookSections: Step 1 (Understand the problem: requirements, back-of-the-envelope estimation); Step 2 (API endpoints, URL redirecting with 301 vs 302, URL shortening overview)

stages.title: Ask before you draw
stages.teaches: The book's prompt is 'design a URL shortener like TinyURL'. Example: https://www.systeminterview.com/q=chatsystem&c=loggedin&v=v3&l=long becomes https://tinyurl.com/y7keocwj, and clicking the short alias redirects to the original. Answers from the book's dialogue: traffic is 100 million URLs generated per day; the short URL should be as short as possible; allowed characters are 0-9, a-z and A-Z; for simplicity, short URLs can't be deleted or updated. Basic use cases: (1) shortening, long URL in, short URL out; (2) redirecting, short URL in, redirect to the long URL. Non-functional needs: high availability, scalability, fault tolerance.
stages.interaction: A 'question deck' of 9 cards. The learner taps the 5 they'd ask the interviewer first. Good cards: 'Can you give an example?', 'What is the traffic volume?', 'How short must the short URL be?', 'Which characters are allowed?', 'Can short URLs be deleted or updated?'. Distractor cards: 'Which programming language?', 'Should I use Kubernetes?', 'What colour is the logo?', 'Should we use MongoDB?'. When a good card is tapped it flips over and shows the interviewer's answer (from the book) in a speech bubble, and that answer is pinned to a 'Requirements' sticky note in the corner, where it stays for later stages. Tapping a distractor gives a gentle shake and a reason ('a tool choice, not a requirement; decide it later'). The stage is done when all 5 good cards are flipped.
stages.check: Q.quiz with 3 questions: (1) Which two use cases make up the core of the system? (shortening + redirecting); (2) What did the interviewer say about deletes/updates? (not allowed, a simplification); (3) Which characters may appear in the short code? (0-9, a-z, A-Z = 62).

stages.title: Napkin math
stages.sub: Back-of-the-envelope, then play with the knobs
stages.teaches: Write ops: 100 million/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,160 per second. Read:write is assumed to be 10:1, so reads ≈ 11,600 per second. Running for 10 years: 100M × 365 × 10 = 365 billion records. With an average URL length of 100 bytes, storage over 10 years = 365 billion × 100 B = 36.5 TB. Tip: round freely (a day ≈ 100k seconds) and say your assumptions out loud.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check: four input boxes (writes/s, reads/s, records in 10 years, storage in 10 years) with unit dropdowns (K/M/B/T and GB/TB). Each answer is accepted within ±10% (writes 1,045–1,275 etc.). Show a 'hint' button per box that reveals the formula. After all four are correct, the boxes turn into live outputs driven by four sliders: URLs/day (10M–1B), read:write ratio (1:1–100:1), years (1–20), average URL bytes (50–500). The learner is asked to answer a mini-challenge: 'Drag the sliders until storage passes 100 TB; which knob moved it fastest?', with no single answer, just reflection text.
stages.check: Stage clears when all four boxes are correct. Short Q.quiz (2 questions): 'If the read:write ratio were 100:1, reads/s ≈ ?' (≈116,000); 'Which number tells you how long the short code must be?' (365 billion records).

stages.title: Two doors in
stages.teaches: REST-style API, two endpoints. (1) URL shortening: POST api/v1/data/shorten, request body {longUrl: longURLString}, returns the shortURL. (2) URL redirecting: GET api/v1/shortUrl, returns the longURL for HTTP redirection. POST because it creates a new resource; GET because a redirect is a read that browsers perform automatically when someone clicks a link.
stages.interaction: Build-the-request: two empty request cards ('Shorten' and 'Redirect'). For each card the learner picks a method chip (GET / POST / PUT / DELETE), a path chip (api/v1/data/shorten, api/v1/{shortUrl}, api/v1/urls/all) and a body chip (none / {longUrl} / {shortUrl}). A 'Send' button fires the request into a mock server that answers with a response panel: correct combos return 200 + shortURL or a 301/302 + Location header; wrong combos return a playful 405/404 with an explanation. Done when both cards return a successful response.
stages.check: Q.quiz with 2 questions: why POST for shorten (creates a new mapping, not idempotent read); what the GET endpoint returns (the long URL inside an HTTP redirect, not a page).

stages.title: 301 or 302?
stages.teaches: When the server receives a short URL it answers with a redirect: a status code plus a Location header holding the long URL. 301 Moved Permanently: the browser caches the response, so later requests for the same short URL go straight to the long URL and never reach the shortener; good for cutting server load. 302 Found (temporarily moved): every request goes to the shortener first, then is redirected; good when analytics matter (click rate, where clicks come from). Interview line: 301 to save load, 302 to track clicks.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch simulation. On screen: a browser (left), the shortener server with a 'requests seen' counter and an 'analytics clicks' counter (middle), and the destination site (right). A toggle selects 301 or 302. Before running, the learner predicts: 'After 3 clicks of the same short link, how many requests will the shortener see?' (choices 0 / 1 / 3). Then they press 'Click link' three times; animated packets travel browser→shortener→browser→destination. With 301, click 1 goes via the shortener, then a 'cached 301' badge appears on the browser and clicks 2–3 jump straight to the destination (counter stays at 1). With 302, every click goes via the shortener (counter 3). The learner must run and predict both codes; a 'Clear browser cache' button resets the browser badge.
stages.check: Both predictions entered and both runs watched (wrong predictions cost no hearts but show the reason). Then Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Marketing wants per-click stats on every click' → 302; 'Which header holds the long URL?' → Location.

stages.title: The obvious version
stages.sub: Step 2 · shortening with a hash table
stages.teaches: The simplest shortening idea: a hash table of <shortURL, longURL> pairs. A hash function fx(longURL) = hashValue, and the short URL is www.tinyurl.com/{hashValue}. Requirements on the function: each long URL must map to one hashValue, and each hashValue must map back to its long URL. This sets up the deep dive: where to store the table (365B rows won't fit in memory) and how to make fx produce short, unique values.
stages.interaction: Mini-sim: a small in-memory table that the learner fills by typing long URLs; each gets a fake 7-char code. A RAM gauge for the server fills based on the 10-year projection (36.5 TB vs a 256 GB server); when the learner clicks 'Fast-forward 10 years' the gauge overflows in red with the message 'In-memory hash table won't hold 365 billion rows; we need a database'. This is a cliff-hanger that hands off to quest 8.2.
stages.check: One Q.quiz question: 'Why can't the whole mapping live in a single server's memory hash table?' (36.5 TB+ over 10 years, far more than one machine's RAM; also lost on restart).

stages.title: Boss: The Redirect Riddler
stages.sub: Pick the right status code for each client
stages.teaches: Applying 301 vs 302 and the estimates to concrete client asks.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'301', label:'301 Moved Permanently', sub:'browser caches it'}, {k:'302', label:'302 Found', sub:'every click hits us'}]. Scenarios (6): marketing team needs click-through rate per campaign → 302; a static docs site, servers are overloaded, nobody reads stats → 301; A/B test that may switch the destination next week → 302; mass printed QR codes on posters pointing to a page that will never move, minimise cost → 301; fraud team wants to see the referrer and country of every click → 302; a link checker crawls the same short URL thousands of times a day and you want to stop paying for it → 301. Each 'why' cites caching vs analytics.
stages.check: Boss cleared when all scenarios answered (engine handles hearts).

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: The first five minutes, out loud
stages.teaches: Pulling scope, estimates, API and redirect choice into one answer.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: interviewer says 'Design a URL shortener like TinyURL. Go.' Placeholder: 'Before I draw anything, I'd like to ask…'. Model answer: 'First I'd scope it: an example, the traffic (say 100M new URLs a day), how short the URL must be, which characters (0-9, a-z, A-Z) and whether links can be deleted (no). Then quick math: about 1,160 writes/s, 10:1 reads so about 11,600 reads/s, 365 billion records over 10 years, about 36.5 TB at 100 bytes each. Two endpoints: POST /api/v1/data/shorten with the long URL, and GET /api/v1/{shortUrl}, which redirects. I'd use 302 if we care about click analytics, 301 if we'd rather the browser cache it to save load.' Checks: ['I asked about traffic, length, characters and deletes before designing', 'I gave writes/s, reads/s, record count and storage', 'I named both endpoints and the 301-vs-302 trade-off'].
stages.check: Self-grade checklist via Q.drill.

caveats: Real shorteners mostly use 301 (bit.ly and TinyURL send 301s) and still collect analytics, because browsers don't cache 301s forever and the first click per browser is logged. The book's '301 = no analytics' is a useful simplification, not a law.
There are also 307 and 308 (like 302 and 301, but the browser must keep the HTTP method). For GET-only redirects, 301 and 302 are fine; mention 307/308 only if asked.
36.5 TB counts only the long URLs. Real storage is higher: short codes, IDs, timestamps, indexes and replicas (×3) multiply it.
10:1 read:write is the book's assumption; popular shorteners are far more read-heavy, which strengthens the case for caching.
The API path GET api/v1/shortUrl is the book's notation; in practice the redirect lives at the root (https://tinyurl.com/{code}) so the short URL stays short.

quests.d: Store the mapping, size the short code, and make hash + collision resolution work
quests.goal: Your win today: you can explain why the short code needs 7 base-62 characters (62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion > 365 billion), how hash + collision resolution works, and why a Bloom filter saves database lookups.
quests.bookSections: Step 3 deep dive: Data model; Hash function: Hash value length; Hash + collision resolution (CRC32/MD5/SHA-1, first 7 chars, append a predefined string, Bloom filter)

stages.title: Out of RAM, into a table
stages.teaches: The in-memory hash table from Step 2 isn't feasible at this size: memory is limited and expensive. The better choice is to store <shortURL, longURL> mappings in a relational database. The book's simplified table 'url' has three columns: id (primary key), shortURL, longURL.
stages.interaction: Schema builder: the learner drags column chips (id, shortURL, longURL, createdAt, userId, clickCount, password) into an empty 'url' table. The target is the book's three columns; extras like createdAt/userId are accepted as 'nice to have, mention in wrap-up' (yellow), while password is rejected with a reason. Then a preview shows three sample rows, including the book's example (2009215674938, zn9edcu, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design).
stages.check: Q.quiz with 2 questions: why move from memory to a DB (memory is limited and costly; 36.5 TB+); which column the redirect path looks up by (shortURL, so it needs an index).

stages.title: How many characters?
stages.sub: Find the smallest n with 62^n ≥ 365 billion
stages.interaction: Predict, then climb: the learner first enters their guess for n. Then a 'length ladder' slider n = 1…8 shows a log-scale bar for 62^n next to a fixed red line at 365 billion, with the exact number printed. When the bar first crosses the line (n=7), it glows green and a counter shows the headroom (3.52T / 365B ≈ 9.6×). A toggle 'only lowercase + digits (36 chars)' shows that you'd need 8 characters (36^7 ≈ 78B < 365B, 36^8 ≈ 2.8T), to show why the alphabet matters.
stages.check: Guess entered and slider explored to n=7. Q.quiz with 2 questions: 62^6 ≈ ? (56.8 billion, not enough); why 62 (digits + lower + upper).

stages.title: Hash it and chop it
stages.sub: CRC32, MD5, SHA-1, then the first 7 characters
stages.teaches: A straightforward approach is to use a well-known hash function. Book example for https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design: CRC32 = 5cb54054 (8 chars), MD5 = 5a62509a84df9ee03fe1230b9df8b84e (32 chars), SHA-1 = 0eeae7916c06853901d9ccbefbfcaf4de57ed85b (40 chars). Even the shortest is longer than 7, so take the first 7 characters of the hash. That causes collisions: two different long URLs can share the first 7 characters.
stages.interaction: Hash lab: an input box pre-filled with the book's Wikipedia URL. Three output rows show CRC32, MD5 and SHA-1 with their length; on the book URL they must match the values above exactly (builder: implement CRC32 inline, SHA-1 via crypto.subtle.digest, and either a small inline MD5 or a precomputed value for the book URL plus 'MD5 not computed live' for other input). A pair of scissors cuts each hash at 7 characters and highlights the kept part. Spot-the-bug panel: 'These hashes are hexadecimal: only 0-9 and a-f. How many 7-character codes does that give?' The learner computes 16^7 = 268,435,456 (accepted within ±5%) and sees that at 100M URLs/day the space fills in under 3 days, unless the hash bits are re-encoded in base 62.
stages.check: 16^7 calculation correct. Q.quiz with 2 questions: why chopping causes collisions (many inputs share a 7-char prefix); what to do about hex (encode the hash bits in base 62 or use more characters).

stages.title: Collision lab
stages.sub: Append a predefined string and try again
stages.teaches: Book's collision resolution: take the first 7 chars of the hash; look the short URL up in the DB; if it already exists (collision), append a predefined string to the long URL and hash again; repeat until there is no collision, then save. It removes collisions, but every attempt is a database query, which is expensive.
stages.interaction: Shrunk-down simulation so collisions are visible: the 'short code' is only 2 characters from a 6-symbol alphabet (36 slots in a grid). The learner adds long URLs from a list (or types their own); each is hashed to a slot with a visible flowchart: hash → 'exists in DB?' → yes: append '#salt' and rehash (slot changes, arrow shows the retry) → no: save. A 'DB queries' counter increments on every lookup. A 'Bulk add 20' button shows the counter climbing faster as the grid fills (show average queries per insert). Predict prompt before bulk add: 'When the grid is 80% full, will an insert take about 1, 2 or 5 lookups on average?' (answer ≈5, since 1/(1−0.8) = 5).
stages.check: Prediction made and bulk add run. Q.quiz with 2 questions: what the 'predefined string' does (changes the input so the hash changes); the hidden cost (a DB lookup per attempt, more as the table fills).

stages.title: The Bloom bouncer
stages.sub: Skip the DB when the answer is 'definitely not'
stages.teaches: A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic technique to test whether an element is in a set. It answers 'definitely not in the set' or 'probably in the set': false positives are possible, false negatives are not. Put it in front of the collision check: 'definitely not' means skip the DB query and use the code; 'probably' means check the DB. It works with adds only, and that fits because our URLs are never deleted.
stages.interaction: Interactive Bloom filter: a row of 32 bits, 3 hash functions. 'Add code' sets 3 bits (animated arrows). 'Check code' lights the 3 bits: if any is 0, a green 'Definitely new, skip the DB' badge; if all are 1, an amber 'Maybe taken, ask the DB' badge. After adding ~8 codes, the learner is challenged to find a false positive: a pre-made list of unused codes, one of which collides on all 3 bits. They predict which badge each will get before checking. A counter shows 'DB queries saved'.
stages.check: Found the false positive. Q.quiz with 2 questions: can a Bloom filter say 'no' wrongly? (no, never a false negative); what happens on 'maybe'? (fall back to the DB check).

stages.title: Boss: The Collision Hydra
stages.sub: Every head you cut grows two more
stages.teaches: Applying length, hashing and collision handling under pressure.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'len', label:'Change code length', sub:'size the space'}, {k:'retry', label:'Append & rehash', sub:'resolve the clash'}, {k:'bloom', label:'Bloom filter', sub:'skip the DB check'}]. Scenarios (6): 'We launched with 6-char codes and 10-year projections say 365B URLs' → len (62^6 = 56.8B too small); 'Two long URLs produced the same first 7 chars' → retry; 'Collision checks make up 60% of DB reads at insert time' → bloom; 'The team uses the first 7 hex chars of MD5 and it's colliding constantly after two days' → len (hex gives only 268M; re-encode in base 62 or lengthen); 'Insert latency spikes as the table fills: more retries, each a DB query' → bloom; 'A new long URL hashes to an existing code; what does the write path do next?' → retry.
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The hash-based answer, compact.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'How long is your short code, and how do you generate it from the long URL?' Placeholder: 'With 62 characters…'. Model: 'I'd store the mapping in a relational table: id, shortURL, longURL. The code uses 62 characters, 0-9, a-z, A-Z. 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, which is short of 365 billion, and 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, so 7 characters. One way is to hash the long URL with something like MD5 and keep 7 characters. That collides, so on a clash I'd append a predefined string and rehash until it's unique. Each check is a DB query, so I'd put a Bloom filter in front: if it says the code definitely isn't used, I skip the DB.' Checks: ['I did 62^n vs 365 billion and landed on 7', 'I explained collisions and append-and-rehash', 'I used a Bloom filter to avoid DB lookups and said it only has false positives'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: The book's 'take the first 7 characters' of a hex hash quietly shrinks the space: hex has 16 symbols, so 16^7 ≈ 268 million codes, which is under 3 days of traffic. A real design base-62-encodes enough hash bits (≈42 bits for 7 chars).
Even with a full 62^7 space, the birthday effect bites: by year 10 (365B of 3.5T slots used), about 1 in 10 new URLs collides on its first try, so retries are routine, not rare.

A Bloom filter for 365 billion entries at a 1% false-positive rate needs ≈9.6 bits per entry ≈ 440 GB. That's much smaller than the data but not a toy; it must be sharded or kept per partition and rebuilt on restart.

Hash-based codes are deterministic, so the same long URL always gets the same code. That is handy for de-duplication, but it means two users shortening the same URL share one link (and its stats) unless you salt with the user ID.
A unique index on shortURL lets the DB itself reject a duplicate insert, which closes the race where two writers pass the 'does it exist?' check at the same moment.

quests.d: Turn a unique ID into a short code with base 62, and weigh it against hashing
quests.goal: Your win today: you can convert an ID to base 62 by hand (11157 → 2TX), explain why it never collides, and compare it with hash + collision resolution, including its weak spot: codes that are easy to guess.
quests.bookSections: Step 3 deep dive: Base 62 conversion; comparison table of hash + collision resolution vs base 62 conversion

stages.title: The 62-digit abacus
stages.teaches: Base conversion is the second approach. Base 62 is used because the code has 62 possible characters. Mapping: 0–9 → '0'–'9', 10–35 → 'a'–'z', 36–61 → 'A'–'Z'. Book example: 11157 (base 10) = 2 × 62² + 55 × 62¹ + 59 × 62⁰ → digits [2, 55, 59] → [2, T, X] → '2TX', so the short URL is https://tinyurl.com/2TX.
stages.interaction: Guided long-division: the screen shows 11157 ÷ 62. The learner types the quotient and remainder for each step (11157 = 179 × 62 + 59; 179 = 2 × 62 + 55; 2 = 0 × 62 + 2). Each remainder drops into a slot, then the learner taps the right character on a 62-key mapping keyboard (59 → X, 55 → T, 2 → 2). The slots read right-to-left, so the final reveal reverses them into '2TX'. A side panel always shows the 0-9/a-z/A-Z mapping strip with indices.
stages.check: All three steps correct. Q.quiz with 2 questions: what index 'a' maps to (10); what index 'A' maps to (36).

stages.title: Decode it back
stages.teaches: Decoding is the reverse: multiply each digit by its power of 62 and add. Because the conversion is one-to-one, every ID has exactly one code and every code has exactly one ID. The book's flow example: ID 2009215674938 → 'zn9edcu'.
stages.interaction: Three decode puzzles with input boxes: '2TX' → 11157; '10' → 62; 'zz' → 35×62+35 = 2205. Then a 'machine mode' toggle where the learner types any number and watches the converter animate both ways, pre-filled with 2009215674938 to show 'zn9edcu' (7 characters).
stages.check: All three decodes correct.

stages.title: Watch the code grow
stages.teaches: With base 62 the short URL length is not fixed; it grows with the ID: IDs below 62 → 1 char, below 3,844 → 2 chars … below 56.8B → 6 chars, up to 3.5T → 7 chars. So early links are very short, and later ones reach 7 characters. It relies on a unique ID generator (Chapter 7).
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch: an 'odometer' counter of IDs with a fast-forward knob (×1, ×1k, ×1M, ×1B per tick) and the live code beside it. Before running, the learner predicts 'At which ID does the code first need 7 characters?' (choices: 365,000,000,000 / 56,800,235,584 / 3,521,614,606,208); the answer is 56,800,235,584 = 62^6. A marker at '100M URLs/day' shows the calendar date when 7-character codes start (≈ day 568, about 1.5 years in, if IDs start at 1). Second toggle: 'Use a Snowflake-style 64-bit ID' and the code jumps to 11 characters (aZl8N0y58M7 at the max), which is the caveat about ID generator choice.
stages.check: Prediction made and the odometer passes 62^6. Q.quiz with 1 question: 'Why does a Snowflake ID give 11-char codes?' (64-bit numbers need log62(2^63) ≈ 10.6 → 11 chars).

stages.title: The guessing game
stages.teaches: Book: if IDs increase by 1 for each new entry, it's easy to figure out the next available short URL, and that is a security concern. Anyone can walk the sequence (2TX, 2TY, 2TZ…) and discover other people's links, some of which point at private documents. Fixes: random or non-sequential IDs, shuffling the ID with a reversible scramble before encoding, longer codes, never putting secrets behind short links, rate limiting the redirect endpoint.
stages.interaction: Role-play: the learner plays an attacker. They're given their own freshly made short link 'tinyurl.com/2TX' and a 'try next code' button. Each press increments the code and reveals a mock destination card (a shared doc, a private map, a meeting link). After 5 presses, a red 'You just enumerated 5 private links' banner appears. Then they switch to defender: toggle 'scramble IDs before encoding' and the attacker's next guesses mostly land on 404s.
stages.check: Q.quiz with 2 questions: why sequential IDs leak (next code is predictable); one mitigation (scramble/randomise IDs, longer codes, rate limiting).

stages.title: Sort the showdown
stages.teaches: Book's comparison table. Hash + collision resolution: fixed short URL length; doesn't need a unique ID generator; collision is possible and must be resolved; it's not possible to figure out the next available short URL because it doesn't depend on an ID. Base 62 conversion: short URL length is not fixed and grows with the ID; depends on a unique ID generator; collision is not possible because the ID is unique; it's easy to figure out the next short URL if the ID increments by 1, which is a security concern. The book picks base 62 for its deep dive.
stages.interaction: Sort game: 8 property cards ('fixed length', 'needs a unique ID generator', 'collisions possible', 'next code is guessable', 'length grows with ID', 'no collisions ever', 'no ID generator needed', 'next code not guessable') to drag or tap into two columns: 'Hash + collision' and 'Base 62'. Wrong drops bounce back with a hint. When done, the completed columns form the book's table.
stages.check: All 8 cards sorted correctly.

stages.title: Boss: The Twin Generators
stages.teaches: Choosing between the two approaches.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'hash', label:'Hash + collision', sub:'fixed length, no ID service'}, {k:'b62', label:'Base 62 of an ID', sub:'unique by construction'}]. Scenarios (6): 'Team has no distributed ID generator and can't build one this quarter' → hash; 'Inserts must never need a retry loop' → b62; 'Short links point to private medical reports' → hash (not guessable; base 62 would need scrambling); 'We want the shortest possible codes for the first year of launch' → b62 (early IDs give 1–5 char codes); 'Security review: competitors must not be able to estimate how many links we create per day' → hash (sequential IDs reveal volume); 'Insert path should do zero DB lookups for uniqueness' → b62.
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Choosing a generation scheme with trade-offs.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Hashing or base 62: which would you pick and why?' Placeholder: 'I'd go with base 62 because…'. Model: 'I'd take a unique ID from a distributed ID generator and base-62 encode it. 11157, for example, becomes 2TX. Since the IDs are unique, there are never collisions and no retry loop. The trade-offs: the code length grows with the ID instead of being fixed, I depend on an ID generator, and sequential IDs make the next code guessable. So I'd scramble the ID before encoding, or use random IDs, and rate-limit the redirect path. Hash plus collision resolution gives fixed-length, unguessable codes with no ID service, but every insert needs a uniqueness check.' Checks: ['I explained base 62 encoding (0-9, a-z, A-Z)', 'I listed the trade-offs from the comparison table', 'I named the guessability risk and a fix'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: The book's example ID 2009215674938 is about 41 bits, which conveniently encodes to 7 characters. A Snowflake ID from Chapter 7 is 64 bits and encodes to 11 characters. To keep codes at 7 characters, real systems use a counter-style generator such as a ticket server, or hand out pre-allocated ID ranges to each web server.
Guessable short links are a real, documented problem: researchers scanned short-URL spaces and found exposed cloud-storage files and map directions ('Gone in Six Characters', 2016).
The book's mapping (a–z before A–Z) is a convention, not a standard. Any fixed order works as long as encode and decode agree.
Base 62 still needs the 'does this long URL already exist?' check if you want one code per long URL; uniqueness of the ID doesn't de-duplicate long URLs.

quests.d: Walk the shortening and redirecting flows, add a cache, and scale it out
quests.goal: Your win today: you can walk through the 6-step shortening flow and the cached redirect flow on a whiteboard, and list the wrap-up talking points: rate limiter, stateless web tier, DB replication and sharding, analytics, availability.
quests.bookSections: Step 3 deep dive: URL shortening deep dive (flow chart, ID 2009215674938 → zn9edcu); URL redirecting deep dive (load balancer, web servers, cache, DB); Step 4 wrap up

stages.title: Order the shortening flow
stages.sub: Six steps, tap them in order
stages.teaches: Book's shortening flow, using base 62: (1) longURL is the input. (2) The system checks whether the longURL is in the database. (3) If it is, it fetches the existing shortURL and returns it. (4) If not, the unique ID generator produces a new unique ID (the primary key). (5) Convert the ID to a shortURL with base 62. (6) Create a new DB row with the ID, shortURL and longURL. Worked example: input https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design, ID 2009215674938, shortURL zn9edcu, saved as one row.
stages.interaction: Tap-in-order widget (custom; an engine Q.order() does not exist yet): 6 shuffled step cards. Correct order lights up a flow chart with a diamond 'longURL in DB?' and yes/no branches. Then a 'Run it' button animates the Wikipedia example through the chart, the ID ticking out of an 'ID generator' box, a base-62 converter turning it into zn9edcu, and a row appearing in a DB table widget.
stages.check: Correct order. Q.quiz with 2 questions: what happens if the long URL was shortened before (return the existing short URL, no new ID); which chapter's component supplies the ID (unique ID generator, Ch. 7).

stages.title: Same URL twice
stages.teaches: The 'is longURL already in the DB?' check makes shortening idempotent: the same long URL returns the same short URL. That needs a fast lookup by longURL, so it needs an index on longURL (often an index on a hash of it, since URLs are long). Without the check, every submit burns a new ID and a new row.
stages.interaction: Mini-sim: a form with a long URL field and a DB table widget. Submit the Wikipedia URL once and a row appears. Before the second submit, the learner predicts 'New row or same short URL?' A toggle 'skip the existence check' lets them see the alternative: duplicate rows pile up with different short codes, and a 'wasted IDs' counter climbs.
stages.check: Prediction made and both modes tried. Q.quiz with 1 question: what index the existence check needs (on longURL, or a hash of it).

stages.title: Bounce with a cache
stages.teaches: Book's redirect flow: (1) a user clicks a short link, e.g. https://tinyurl.com/zn9edcu; (2) the load balancer forwards the request to a web server; (3) if the shortURL is in the cache, return the longURL directly; (4) if not, fetch the longURL from the DB; if it isn't in the DB either, the user probably entered an invalid short URL; (5) the longURL is returned to the user (as a redirect). Since reads far outnumber writes (10:1), the <shortURL, longURL> mapping is kept in a cache for speed.
stages.interaction: Traffic simulation: user icons → load balancer → 3 web servers → cache → DB. A 'traffic' slider (100 → 11,600 req/s) and a 'cache on/off' toggle. Requests follow a skewed popularity distribution (a few hot links get most clicks). Gauges: cache hit ratio, DB reads/s and a DB 'heat' bar that turns red above capacity (say 3,000 reads/s). With cache off at 11,600 req/s the DB overheats; with cache on, hit ratio rises to ~80–90% and the DB cools. A 'click an unknown code' button sends a request that misses cache and DB and returns a 404 card. Predict first: 'With the cache on at 11,600 req/s, will the DB stay under 3,000 reads/s?' (yes).
stages.check: Ran both cache modes and the invalid-code path. Q.quiz with 2 questions: what the cache stores (shortURL → longURL); what happens when the code is in neither cache nor DB (invalid short URL, return 404).

stages.title: Wrap-up arsenal
stages.sub: Step 4 · what to add with leftover time
stages.teaches: The book's wrap-up talking points: Rate limiter: a malicious user could send an overwhelming number of shortening requests; filter by IP address or other rules (Chapter 4). Web server scaling: the web tier is stateless, so add or remove servers easily. Database scaling: replication and sharding. Analytics: integrate an analytics solution so you know how many people click, when and from where. Availability, consistency and reliability: core concepts for any large system (Chapter 1).
stages.interaction: Match game: 6 problem cards ('A bot submits 50k URLs a minute', 'Black Friday traffic triples overnight', 'Single DB is at 36 TB and growing', 'Marketing asks which campaign drove clicks', 'Primary DB crashes at 3am', 'Cache node dies and reads spike') to tap-match with fix cards (rate limiter, add stateless web servers, shard by shortURL, analytics pipeline (log clicks with 302), DB replication with failover, cache replicas plus a DB that can absorb a warm-up). Each correct match pins the fix onto a growing architecture diagram, so the learner ends with the full final design on screen.
stages.check: All 6 matched. Q.quiz with 1 question: why the web tier scales easily (stateless; all state lives in DB/cache).

stages.title: Boss: The 3 a.m. Pager
stages.teaches: Failure follow-ups for the final design.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'cache', label:'Cache layer', sub:'hot reads'}, {k:'db', label:'DB replication / sharding', sub:'durable mapping'}, {k:'rl', label:'Rate limiter', sub:'abuse control'}, {k:'web', label:'Scale web tier', sub:'stateless servers'}]. Scenarios (7): 'A viral tweet sends 200k clicks/min to one short link' → cache; 'A spam botnet creates millions of short links to phishing pages' → rl; 'The primary DB server dies and redirects start failing' → db (replica takes over); 'The data has outgrown one machine' → db (shard by shortURL/ID); 'Morning traffic doubles and web servers hit 90% CPU' → web; 'Someone scrapes codes sequentially, 1,000 lookups/s from one IP' → rl; 'p99 redirect latency is 200 ms because every click reads the DB' → cache.
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Walking both paths and the scale story.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Walk me through what happens when someone shortens a URL, and when someone clicks the short link.' Placeholder: 'To shorten, the request hits…'. Model: 'Shortening: the API server checks whether the long URL is already in the DB; if so it returns the existing short URL. If not, it gets a new ID from the distributed ID generator, base-62 encodes it, for example 2009215674938 becomes zn9edcu, and stores id, shortURL and longURL. Redirecting: the click goes through a load balancer to a stateless web server, which checks the cache for the short URL, falls back to the DB on a miss, returns 404 if it isn't found, and otherwise sends a 301 or 302 to the long URL. To scale, I'd add a rate limiter on shortening, more web servers, DB replicas and sharding by short URL, plus click analytics.' Checks: ['I described the shortening flow including the existence check', 'I described the redirect flow with cache-then-DB and the 404 case', 'I mentioned at least three of rate limiting, web scaling, DB replication/sharding, analytics'].
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill.

caveats: The book doesn't size the cache. A common rule of thumb is to cache the hot 20% of daily reads. At ~1 billion reads/day that's a few tens of GB of mappings, which fits in a small Redis/Memcached cluster.
Because links are never updated or deleted, the cache is easy to keep correct: an entry can never go stale. Adding edit/delete (a common follow-up) brings back cache invalidation.

Sharding by short URL (or ID) keeps the redirect a single-shard lookup, but the 'is longURL already stored?' check then needs a separate index keyed by longURL or its hash, or it becomes a scatter-gather query.
If the DB uses async replication, a just-created short link might briefly 404 when read from a lagging replica. Read your own writes from the primary, or write-through the cache on create.

quests.d: Full mock interview: design a URL shortener in 45 minutes
quests.goal: Your win today: you can run the whole interview, from scoping questions and estimates through API, 301/302, data model, 7-char base-62 codes, both flows and caching, to failure follow-ups and wrap-up, without notes.
quests.bookSections: Whole chapter via the 4-step framework: Step 1 scope + estimates; Step 2 API, 301/302, hash table; Step 3 data model, hash length, hash vs base 62, shortening + redirecting deep dives; Step 4 wrap up

stages.title: Scope it
stages.teaches: Requirements: 100M URLs/day, as short as possible, [0-9a-zA-Z], no delete/update, use cases shorten + redirect, high availability/scalability/fault tolerance. Estimates: ~1,160 writes/s, ~11,600 reads/s, 365B records, 36.5 TB.
stages.interaction: Interview chat UI like 0008: the interviewer bubble says 'Design a URL shortener.' The learner gets a timer-styled budget of 5 'question tokens' and a deck of 10 possible questions (mix of strong, weak, and premature-implementation ones). Each strong pick gets an interviewer reply that lands on the requirement board; weak picks cost a token with a coach note. Then a rapid estimate round: four multiple-choice estimates (writes/s, reads/s, records, storage) each with 3 options within an order of magnitude; a 'show work' toggle explains each.
stages.check: Requirement board has the 5 key facts; all 4 estimates correct (retry allowed). Scorecard records how many tokens were wasted.

stages.title: Sketch it
stages.sub: Step 2 · high-level design and buy-in (10–15 min)
stages.teaches: Two endpoints (POST api/v1/data/shorten {longUrl}, GET api/v1/{shortUrl}); redirect via 301 (cached, less load) or 302 (every click hits us, analytics); shortening as a hash function fx mapping longURL → hashValue.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard builder: drag boxes (Client, Load balancer, Web servers, Cache, Database, ID generator, Rate limiter, Kafka, CDN) onto a canvas and connect them; the 'interviewer' asks for buy-in at the end. Minimum correct high-level: Client → LB → Web servers → Cache + DB, with ID generator attached to web servers. Extras like Rate limiter are accepted and noted for wrap-up; Kafka/CDN get 'not needed yet; why?' notes. Then the interviewer asks 'Which redirect code?' and the learner must pick 301 or 302 and a reason chip matching the requirement (analytics → 302, load → 301; both accepted if reason matches).
stages.check: Diagram has the required boxes and edges; redirect choice paired with a matching reason.

stages.title: Dig in
stages.sub: Step 3 · data model, code length, generation
stages.teaches: Relational table (id, shortURL, longURL); 62^7 ≈ 3.5T ≥ 365B → 7 chars; hash + collision resolution (first 7 chars, append string, Bloom filter) vs base 62 of a unique ID (no collisions, variable length, guessable); the book picks base 62; shortening flow (check longURL exists → new ID → base 62 → save) and redirect flow (LB → web → cache → DB → 404 if missing).
stages.interaction: Three rapid deep-dive panels the interviewer 'zooms into'. (a) Schema: pick the 3 columns. (b) Length: slider n with 62^n readout; lock in n=7. (c) Generation: choose hash+collision or base 62; whichever is chosen, the interviewer pushes back with that approach's weak spot (hash → 'collisions cost DB lookups, now what?' expecting Bloom filter; base 62 → 'I can guess the next link, now what?' expecting scramble/random IDs + rate limit). Then a tap-in-order of the combined shortening flow (6 steps) and redirect flow (5 steps).
stages.check: All three panels answered and both flows ordered; pushback answered with an accepted mitigation.

stages.title: Boss: the curveball barrage
stages.teaches: Failure and extension follow-ups across the whole design.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'cache', label:'Cache it', sub:'hot reads'}, {k:'data', label:'Replicate / shard', sub:'DB tier'}, {k:'guard', label:'Rate limit / validate', sub:'protect the system'}, {k:'design', label:'Rethink the code scheme', sub:'length/generation'}]. Scenarios (8): one link goes viral → cache; DB primary dies → data; 365B rows don't fit one box → data; bots mass-create links → guard; users enumerate sequential codes → design (scramble/random IDs) and say rate limiting helps too; the interviewer says traffic is 10× (1B URLs/day for 10 years = 3.65T > 62^7) → design (go to 8 chars); a user pastes a link to a known malware site → guard (validate against a blocklist); the cache cluster restarts cold and the DB is hammered → cache (warm up / replicas, plus DB read replicas).
stages.check: Boss cleared.

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.teaches: Wrap-up points: rate limiter, web server scaling (stateless), DB scaling (replication + sharding), analytics, availability/consistency/reliability; plus honest bottleneck call-outs (ID generator as a dependency, Bloom filter size, guessable codes).
stages.interaction: Pick-5 from 9 wrap-up cards in 30 seconds (soft timer, no penalty after it runs out except a scorecard note). Strong: rate limiter; stateless web tier; DB replication; DB sharding; analytics; caveat on guessable IDs. Weak: 'rewrite in Rust', 'add blockchain', 'switch to GraphQL'. The interviewer reacts to each pick.
stages.check: At least 4 strong picks.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The full chapter as one elevator answer.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'You have 60 seconds. Summarise your URL shortener design.' Model: 'Scope: 100M new URLs a day, short codes from 0-9, a-z, A-Z, and links are never edited. That's about 1,160 writes/s, 11,600 reads/s, 365 billion rows and about 36.5 TB over 10 years. API: POST to shorten, GET on the short code to redirect, using 302 if we want click analytics and 301 to offload traffic. Storage: a table of id, shortURL, longURL. Codes: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, so 7 characters, made by base-62 encoding a unique ID from a distributed ID generator, so there are no collisions; I'd scramble the ID so codes can't be guessed. Shortening first checks whether the long URL already exists. Redirects go LB → stateless web servers → cache → DB, with a 404 for unknown codes. For scale and safety: a rate limiter, DB replication and sharding by code, and click analytics.' Checks: ['Scope and the four estimates', 'API + 301/302 trade-off', '7 chars from 62^7 and the generation scheme with its trade-off', 'Both flows including cache and existence check', 'Wrap-up: rate limiter, scaling, analytics']. After the drill, show a scorecard (tokens wasted in stage 1, pushback answered, boss hearts, wrap-up picks) and save it under a separate localStorage key 'sdq:v1:<this quest id>-interview', as 0008 does.
stages.check: Self-grade via Q.drill; scorecard rendered.

caveats: The book picks base 62 conversion for its deep dive but doesn't spell out the guessability fix; interviewers often probe it, so have 'scramble or randomise the ID' ready.
Real shorteners (bit.ly, TinyURL) use 301 and still collect analytics; the book's 301-vs-302 framing is an interview simplification.
With 7 characters there is only ~9.6× headroom over 365 billion; if the interviewer scales traffic 10×, you need 8 characters.
To keep 7-char codes, the ID generator must produce compact counter-style IDs (ticket server or range allocation); a 64-bit Snowflake ID gives 11-char codes.

cheatsheetOutline: Title: World 8, Design a URL Shortener (one page). §8.1 Scope & API: requirements (100M URLs/day, shortest possible, [0-9a-zA-Z], no delete/update, shorten + redirect, HA/scalable/fault-tolerant); key numbers box (1,160 writes/s; 11,600 reads/s at 10:1; 365B records in 10 yrs; 36.5 TB at 100 B/URL); endpoints POST api/v1/data/shorten {longUrl} and GET api/v1/{shortUrl}; 301 (browser caches, less load) vs 302 (every click hits us, analytics) with the Location header. §8.2 Length & hashing: table url(id, shortURL, longURL); 62^n ladder (62^6 = 56.8B < 365B ≤ 62^7 = 3.52T, so n = 7); CRC32/MD5/SHA-1 lengths (8/32/40 hex) with the book example; first 7 chars → collisions → append a predefined string and rehash; Bloom filter = 'definitely not' or 'maybe', no false negatives; caveat that 16^7 = 268M hex space. §8.3 Base 62: mapping 0-9 / a-z (10–35) / A-Z (36–61); worked example 11157 = 2·62² + 55·62 + 59 → 2TX; 2009215674938 → zn9edcu; comparison table (hash: fixed length, no ID gen, collisions, not guessable; base 62: variable length, needs ID gen, no collisions, guessable → scramble); Snowflake → 11 chars caveat. §8.4 Flows & scale: 6-step shortening flow chart; 5-step redirect flow (LB → web → cache → DB → 404); wrap-up list (rate limiter, stateless web tier, DB replication + sharding, analytics, availability/consistency/reliability). Final design diagram: Client → Load balancer → stateless Web servers (+ rate limiter, ID generator) → Cache (shortURL→longURL) → Database (replicated, sharded by code), with an analytics side-stream. Footer: 'What happens when…?' quick answers (viral link, DB primary dies, bots, enumeration, 10× traffic → 8 chars).
